Fitting means minimising $-2 \log L$, here with the prior $-2 \log$ of the posterior, over the outer
parameters. The objective of an ODE model is smooth but rarely convex: it has local optima, flat
directions and regions where the model cannot be evaluated. dMod2 [@kaschek2019dmod] fits with a
trust-region method on the exact gradient, `trust()`, and runs it from many starts, `mstrust()`.
This chapter describes the method and every setting of the two functions, fits the model of
[chapter 1](guide-model.html) with the gauge of [chapter 2](guide-symmetries.html), compares the
sources of the model Hessian on two published problems, and covers the two variants of the
method: L1 penalties by `trustL1()` and multiple shooting. The code of the fits is `fit.R` and
`plots.R` of the project.

## Trust region

At the iterate $\theta_k$ with the gradient $g$ and a symmetric approximation $H$ of the Hessian,
`trust()` minimises the quadratic model of the objective inside a ball,

$$\min_{s} \; m(s) = g^\top s + \tfrac{1}{2}\, s^\top H s \quad \text{subject to} \quad \lVert s \rVert \le r .$$

The ratio of the actual to the predicted decrease decides whether the step is taken and how the
radius $r$ changes. Far from the optimum the radius keeps the steps where the quadratic model
holds; near it the steps are Newton steps of the model, with fast local convergence. The
subproblem solver, the radius update, the bounds and the termination tests below are the same
for every source of $H$.

### Subproblem

`trust()` solves the subproblem exactly, through the full eigendecomposition of $H$
[@more1983computing]. The solution satisfies $(H + \nu I)\, s = -g$ with a multiplier $\nu \ge 0$
that makes $H + \nu I$ positive semidefinite and vanishes unless the step reaches the boundary,
$\lVert s \rVert = r$. With $H = Q \Lambda Q^\top$, eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ and $\gamma = Q^\top g$,
the step

$$s(\nu) = -Q (\Lambda + \nu I)^{-1} \gamma$$

solves the subproblem when $\nu \ge \max(0, -\lambda_{\min})$ and either $\nu = 0$ with
$\lVert s \rVert \le r$, or $\nu > 0$ with $\lVert s \rVert = r$. The second case is a root of the
secular equation

$$\phi(\nu) = \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{\lVert s(\nu) \rVert}
 = \frac{1}{r} - \Big( \sum_i \frac{\gamma_i^2}{(\lambda_i + \nu)^2} \Big)^{-1/2},$$

which is smooth and almost linear for $\nu > -\lambda_{\min}$, so Newton's method on $\phi$
converges in a few iterations, each $O(n_\theta)$ once the eigendecomposition is known. When
$\gamma_i = 0$ for every eigenvector of $\lambda_{\min} < 0$, no $\nu$ drives $\lVert s \rVert$ out
to $r$ (the hard case), and the solution is $s(-\lambda_{\min}) + \tau q_{\min}$ with $\tau$ chosen
so that $\lVert s \rVert = r$. A positive definite $H$ never reaches the hard case; an indefinite
quasi-Newton model can.

The exact solution handles an indefinite $H$ directly: a direction of negative curvature is followed
to the boundary. The eigendecomposition costs $O(n_\theta^3)$ per iteration; for a large model with
a sparse Hessian the sparse path below factorises instead.

### Step and radius

Each iteration compares the decrease the model predicts with the actual one,

$$\rho_k = \frac{f(\theta_k) - f(\theta_k + s_k)}{-m_k(s_k)},$$

and updates the radius from it, with $r_{\max}$ = `rmax`:

$$r_{k+1} = \begin{cases}
\min(r_k/4,\, \lVert s_k \rVert / 4), & \rho_k < 1/4, \\
\min(2 r_k,\, r_{\max}), & \rho_k > 3/4 \text{ and } \lVert s_k \rVert \ge 0.9\, r_k, \\
r_k, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}$$

A step with $\rho_k < 1/4$ is rejected, and a rejected step much shorter than the radius shrinks
the radius to the step's own scale. The radius grows only when the step reached the boundary,
since a shorter step was limited by the model, not by the region. The first radius is `rinit`,
in the units of the parameters: on the natural log scale of the Oppelt model, `rinit = 0.1` is a
first step of ten percent in a rate constant.

A trial point at which the objective fails, for example because the ODE solver gives up, or
returns a value that is not finite, counts as rejected and quarters the radius. Three failures in
a row end the run with `stopReason = "objfun"`. A fit therefore needs no bounds to keep it out of
regions where the model cannot be evaluated: it backs off from them.

### Nonmonotone acceptance

With `stepControl$nonmonotone` $= \eta \in (0, 1)$, the actual decrease is measured from a
weighted average of past values [@zhang2004nonmonotone],

$$Q_{k+1} = \eta Q_k + 1, \qquad C_{k+1} = \frac{\eta Q_k C_k + f(\theta_{k+1})}{Q_{k+1}},$$

and $\rho_k = \bigl(C_k - f(\theta_k + s_k)\bigr) / \bigl(-m_k(s_k)\bigr)$. At $\eta = 0$, the
default, $C_k = f(\theta_k)$ and the rule above is recovered. A larger $\eta$ lets the iterate
leave a narrow valley by accepting steps that raise the objective, so the result reports the best
iterate visited, not the last. The termination tests read the objective itself: only the
acceptance is relaxed.

### Bounds

`parlower` and `parupper` bound the parameters, named or as one number for all. The default,
`boundary = "reflective"`, is the interior trust-region method of Coleman and Li
[@coleman1996interior], which turns a bound into a change of metric. With $v_i$ the signed
distance from $\theta_i$ to the bound the gradient pushes it towards (1 if that bound is
infinite), $D = \operatorname{diag}(\lvert v \rvert^{1/2})$ and $J^v$ the diagonal of
$\partial \lvert v \rvert / \partial \theta$, the subproblem is solved in the scaled variables

$$\hat g = D g, \qquad \hat B = D H D + \operatorname{diag}(g)\, J^v ,$$

so the model steepens towards a bound and the step turns away from it. The first-order optimality
measure that `gtol` reads, $\max_i \lvert v_i g_i \rvert$, vanishes both at an interior stationary
point and at a bound the gradient pushes into. A step that would still leave the box is cut to the
fraction `stepControl$thetaMax` (default 0.99995) of the distance to the bound, reflected off the
blocking faces, or replaced by the scaled steepest-descent step, whichever the model rates best.
Every iterate stays strictly inside the box; `atBound` in the result names the parameters a bound
holds. A start outside the box is moved inside with a warning.

`boundary = "clip"` reduces the subproblem to the parameters that are free, those not at a bound
the gradient pushes into, and clips the step componentwise. It returns a shorter result and
supports no quasi-Newton source. On the log scale with a prior, as in the Oppelt model, every
parameter moves freely and the fit needs no bounds.

### Termination

The run stops as soon as one of the following tests holds; `stopReason` in the result names it.
The gradient test is evaluated at the current iterate, the value and step tests on an accepted
step.

| `stopReason` | test | `converged` |
|---|---|---|
| `"gradient"` | $\max_i \lvert v_i g_i \rvert \le$ `gtol`; without bounds $\max_i \lvert g_i \rvert$ | `TRUE` |
| `"fvalue"` | an accepted step changed the value by less than `ftol` | `TRUE` |
| `"preddiff"` | the model predicts a decrease below `mtol`, also on a rejected Newton step inside the region | `TRUE` |
| `"step"` | the step norm is below `xtol` (default 0, off) | `TRUE` |
| `"stagnation"` | five rejected steps in a row left the value flat within `ftol` | `TRUE` |
| `"radius"` | the radius fell below `rmin` (default 0, off) | `FALSE` |
| `"objfun"` | three failed evaluations in a row | `FALSE` |
| `"iterlim"` | `iterlim` iterations | `FALSE` |

Only `"gradient"` tests first-order optimality. `"fvalue"`, `"preddiff"` and `"step"` read the
prediction of the quadratic model, so a model Hessian that misrepresents the local curvature can
end a run at a point that is not stationary, with `converged = TRUE` at a value above the
optimum. In a quasi-Newton phase, where the model is an approximation still being built, the three
are not applied: such a phase ends on the gradient, on stagnation, which counts rejected steps
instead of reading the model, or on the radius. The gradient norm is the stopping test usually
recommended for quasi-Newton methods [@nocedal2006numerical].

The tolerances are bounded below by what the objective resolves. For an ODE model integrated at
relative tolerance $\epsilon$, the value has a relative error of about $\epsilon$ and the
sensitivities about an order more, which gives the gradient a noise floor. `ftol` belongs at or
above $\epsilon \lvert f \rvert$, and `gtol` at the noise floor of the gradient; a tighter
tolerance needs a tighter integrator first. A run that ends on `"stagnation"` rather than on
`"gradient"` points to tolerances below the noise floor; `max(abs(fit$gradient))` shows where it
lies. `model.R` sets `ftol`, `mtol` and `gtol` above the error of the solver, as
[chapter 1](guide-model.html#solver-error) measures it, and passes them as `tolControl`.

## Model Hessian

`hessianMethod` selects the source of $H$:

| value | $H$ | the objective returns |
|---|---|---|
| `"gn"` | the Gauss-Newton Hessian, at every iterate | value, gradient, Gauss-Newton Hessian |
| `"exact"` | the exact Hessian, at every iterate: a Newton run | value, gradient, exact Hessian |
| `"bfgs"` | a damped BFGS update [@powell1978fast] | value, gradient |
| `"sr1"` | a symmetric rank-one update, possibly indefinite | value, gradient |

### Gauss-Newton

$H$ is by default the Gauss-Newton matrix. With the residuals $r_j = (y_j - f_j)/\sigma_j$ and their
Jacobian $J$ from the sensitivities, the Hessian of $\sum_j r_j^2$ is

$$\nabla^2 \sum_j r_j^2 = 2 J^\top J + 2 \sum_j r_j \nabla^2 r_j .$$

The second term needs the second-order sensitivities and is small where the model fits, with
residuals that scatter around zero; Gauss-Newton keeps the first, which is positive semidefinite
and free: the Jacobian that gives the gradient also gives $J^\top J$, so an iteration with the
Hessian costs no more than one with the gradient alone. The prior adds its exact Hessian,
$2/s_k^2$ on the diagonal. With an error model that depends on the parameters, the matrix
also has first-order terms of the variance, which need not be positive semidefinite
([chapter 3](guide-sensitivities.html)).

Near an optimum with large residuals the Gauss-Newton model, without the second term, stops
improving, and `ftol` or `mtol` ends the run short of the minimum. A quasi-Newton approximation
infers the curvature from the steps taken and has no such bias.

### Exact Hessian

`hessianMethod = "exact"` asks the objective for its exact Hessian at every iterate,
`obj(..., deriv2 = TRUE)`, and runs Newton's method in the trust region, which takes an indefinite
Hessian as it comes. It needs the second-order sensitivities of the whole chain: models built with
`deriv2 = TRUE`, or with the derivative mode `"forward-reverse"` and evaluated backwards,
see [chapter 3](guide-sensitivities.html). An iteration costs far more than with the Gauss-Newton
Hessian, but the model is exact wherever the residuals are large.

### BFGS

Both quasi-Newton updates use the secant pair

$$s_k = \theta_{k+1} - \theta_k, \qquad y_k = \nabla f(\theta_{k+1}) - \nabla f(\theta_k),$$

and require the new model to reproduce it, $B_{k+1} s_k = y_k$. BFGS is the rank-two update that
keeps $B$ positive definite, which requires $s^\top y > 0$. Away from a minimum this curvature
condition can fail, so the pair is damped before use [@powell1978fast]: with

$$\vartheta = \begin{cases}
1, & s^\top y \ge 0.2\, s^\top B s, \\
\dfrac{0.8\, s^\top B s}{s^\top B s - s^\top y}, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\qquad \tilde y = \vartheta y + (1 - \vartheta) B s ,$$

the update is

$$B_{k+1} = B_k - \frac{B_k s\, s^\top B_k}{s^\top B_k s} + \frac{\tilde y\, \tilde y^\top}{s^\top \tilde y}.$$

The damped pair satisfies $s^\top \tilde y \ge 0.2\, s^\top B s > 0$, so $B$ stays positive
definite. `qnControl$qnCautious` adds the test of Li and Fukushima [@li2001modified]: a pair
counts only when $s^\top y > c \lVert s \rVert \lVert y \rVert$ with $c$ = `qnCautious` (default
`1e-8`), which discards pairs whose curvature is numerical noise; `qnSkipped` in the result
counts them. BFGS updates from accepted steps only.

### SR1

SR1 is the rank-one update that satisfies the secant equation without requiring definiteness.
With $w = y - B_k s$,

$$B_{k+1} = B_k + \frac{w\, w^\top}{w^\top s},$$

the only symmetric rank-one correction that does so. Since $w^\top s$ can be arbitrarily small,
the update is skipped when $\lvert w^\top s \rvert \le 10^{-8} \lVert s \rVert \lVert w \rVert$.
SR1 converges to the true Hessian, indefinite regions included, and the subproblem solver steps
along the negative curvature it reports. A rejected trial point still supplies a valid pair, because
the curvature along a step does not depend on whether the step is accepted, and its gradient is
already computed [@nocedal2006numerical]; `qnControl$qnRejected`, `TRUE` for `"sr1"`, uses it.

### Seed and memory

The quasi-Newton settings are entries of `qnControl` and apply to a `"bfgs"` or `"sr1"` phase:

| entry | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `hessianInit` | `"gn"` | the seed: the Gauss-Newton Hessian at the start, `"identity"`, or `"exact"`, the exact Hessian at the start and gradients only after it |
| `hessianReseed` | `"never"` | `"stall"`: a quasi-Newton phase that would stop on stagnation starts again from a fresh seed of the same kind at the current iterate, if the iterate moved since the last reseed, at most eight times per phase |
| `qnMemory` | `0` | `0` accumulates every update onto the seed; a positive number rebuilds the approximation in each iteration from the last `qnMemory` pairs |
| `qnCautious` | `1e-8` | the cautious test of BFGS; `0` turns it off |
| `qnRejected` | `TRUE` for `"sr1"` | SR1 also updates from rejected trial points |

With `hessianInit = "identity"`, `trust()` never asks for a Hessian, so an objective that returns
gradients alone suffices. The Gauss-Newton seed is not always the better one: far from the optimum
$J^\top J$ is large and severely ill-conditioned. A BFGS update is of rank two and keeps $B$
positive definite, so where the seed is wrong by orders of magnitude the wrong curvature dominates
the approximation for many steps. SR1 has no sign constraint and overwrites such curvature
outright. The comparison below measures both.

With `qnMemory` $= m > 0$ the approximation is rebuilt in each iteration from $\gamma I$ and the
most recent $m$ pairs, with $\gamma = y^\top y / s^\top y$ of the newest pair, the scaling of
Shanno and Phua [@shanno1978matrix]. This is the curvature information of L-BFGS
[@nocedal2006numerical], assembled into the explicit matrix the subproblem needs. It saves no
memory; the seed and every pair older than the last $m$ are forgotten.

`trust()` has no diagonal preconditioner and no scaled identity as seed. On a logarithmic
parameter scale, the normal case in dMod2, a diagonal scaling has nothing to correct, and the
ill-conditioning of sloppy models lies along rotated directions [@gutenkunst2007universally] that
no diagonal scaling reaches.

### Phases

`phases` lists Hessian sources that a run passes through one after the other. Each phase is a
list with its own `hessianMethod`, and optionally its own `iterlim`, `sweep` and `qnControl`,
merged over the top-level `qnControl`. A run stays in a phase until a value, model, step or
stagnation stop, or the phase's own `iterlim`, would end it, and then hands over to the next
phase instead. `"gradient"` stays terminal: it is an optimality test, not a symptom of a stalled
model. A handover restarts the radius at `rinit` and discards the quasi-Newton pairs; a
quasi-Newton phase after the first starts from the Gauss-Newton Hessian at the iterate of the
handover. `switches` bounds the number of handovers: by default one fewer than there are phases,
so each runs once; a higher value cycles through the list again, `0` runs the first phase only.
The construction follows Fides of Fröhlich and Sorger [@froehlich2022fides], which switches from
one Hessian source to another when the trust region stops making progress.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Gauss-Newton until the model stops improving, then SR1 to the stationary point
fit <- trust(obj, best, fixed = gauge, tolControl = tolerances,
             phases = list(list(hessianMethod = "gn"), list(hessianMethod = "sr1")))
fit[c("phaseIterations", "evalBySource", "nSwitch", "stopReason")]
```

Without `phases` a run has one source, from `hessianMethod` and `qnControl`; with `phases`,
`hessianMethod` is an error. Names of the list label the phases in the result. `phaseIterations`
holds the iterations of each phase run in order, `evalBySource` the evaluations per source,
`qnEval` those in a quasi-Newton phase, `nSwitch` the handovers.

### Reverse sweep

A quasi-Newton phase needs the gradient alone. With `sweep = "reverse"` the objective computes it
by one backward sweep of the adjoint system instead of the $n_\theta$ sensitivity columns of the
forward sweep, for models built with `derivMode = c("forward", "reverse")`;
[chapter 3](guide-sensitivities.html) describes the sweep and its accuracy. The `sweep` of a phase
is an entry of the phase. Left out, a `"bfgs"` or `"sr1"` phase runs backwards if the objective
can be evaluated backwards at the start, forwards otherwise; a Gauss-Newton phase always runs
forwards, since $J^\top J$ needs the forward sensitivities. `phaseSweep` in the result reports the
sweep of every phase. Without `phases`, a `sweep` passed to `trust()` goes to the objective as is.

### Sparse Hessians

For a model with many parameters that each act on few conditions, such as a fit over hundreds of
cell lines with their own parameters, the Gauss-Newton Hessian is sparse. `sparse = TRUE` asks
the objective for it as a sparse `Matrix` and solves the subproblem by sparse Cholesky factors of
$H + \nu I$, with Newton's method on $1/\lVert s(\nu) \rVert = 1/r$. The default `"auto"` takes
this path for a Gauss-Newton minimisation without phases, bounds, exact Hessian, trace or multiple
shooting when there are at least 500 parameters and the Hessian at the start fills at most 5 % of
the matrix; `options(dMod2.sparseAuto = list(parameters = , fill = ))` changes both thresholds.

### Arguments and result

| argument | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `rinit`, `rmax` | `0.1`, `10` | first and largest radius, in the units of the parameters |
| `iterlim` | `1000` | iterations over all phases |
| `hessianMethod` | `"gn"` | `"gn"`, `"exact"`, `"bfgs"` or `"sr1"`, see Model Hessian |
| `phases`, `switches` | none | a run over several Hessian sources, see Phases |
| `parlower`, `parupper` | none | bounds |
| `boundary` | `"reflective"` | `"reflective"` or `"clip"`, see Bounds |
| `tolControl` | `ftol`, `mtol`, `gtol` `1e-6`; `xtol`, `rmin` `0`; `ctol` `1e-6` | the termination tests; `ctol` for multiple shooting |
| `qnControl` | see Seed and memory | the quasi-Newton update |
| `stepControl` | `thetaMax = 0.99995`, `nonmonotone = 0` | the step; further entries for multiple shooting |
| `minimize` | `TRUE` | `FALSE` maximises |
| `sparse` | `"auto"` | the sparse path |
| `blather` | `FALSE` | `TRUE` returns the trace of every iteration |
| `printIter` | `FALSE` | print the value at each evaluation |
| `traceFile` | none | a CSV file with one row per evaluation: iteration, value, parameters |

An argument `trust()` does not know goes to the objective, such as `fixed`, the parameters held
at given values. A flat `ftol = ` or `hessianInit = ` is an error that names the control list it
belongs to, and an unknown entry of a control list is an error.

The result, of class `trustfit`, holds the best iterate `argument` with its `value`, `gradient`
and model `hessian`, the counts `iterations` and `neval`, `converged`, `atBound` and
`stopReason`, and the quasi-Newton and phase counts above. With `blather = TRUE` it also holds
`argpath` and `argtry`, the accepted iterates and trial points, and per iteration `steptype`,
`stepback`, `accept`, the radius `r`, `rho`, `valpath`, `valtry`, `preddiff`, `stepnorm` and, with
a quasi-Newton source, `hessianSource`. `vcov(fit)` inverts half the Hessian for the covariance
of the estimate, without the parameters a bound holds.

## One fit

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !fitted}
cat("> Results pending: `results/fits.rds` of the project is written by `fit.R`.\n")
```

A fit from a start near the best fit, with the gauge held fixed. `mstrust()` with one fit draws the
start, here with standard deviation 0.5 around the best fit, and draws again where the model cannot
be evaluated, for example where the resting state of the cells is no longer stable:

```{r, eval = fitted}
best <- as.parvec(readRDS("results/fits.rds"))
set.seed(1)
fit <- mstrust(obj, best, fixed = gauge, sd = 0.5, fits = 1, rinit = 0.1, rmax = 10,
               iterlim = 1000, tolControl = tolerances)[[1]]
fit[c("value", "converged", "iterations", "stopReason")]
```

## Multistart

A single fit finds the optimum whose basin of attraction contains its start. `mstrust()` fits from
many starts, drawn around a centre, and returns them as a list of fits; `as.parframe()` turns it into
a table sorted by value. `fit.R` draws the starts from the prior means with standard deviation 2 on
the log scale, a factor of $e^2 \approx 7$ per standard deviation. A start at which the model
cannot be evaluated, for example because a bleaching rate is so large that a signal vanishes, is
replaced by the next draw. `cores` runs the fits in parallel processes.

```{r multistart, eval = FALSE}
```

`mstrust()` sorts its arguments by name: those of the optimiser go to `trust()`, those of the
sampler, by default `rnorm()` with its `sd`, to the sampler, every other one to the objective.
Every start, those of the retries included, is drawn before the fits are spread over the cores,
so `set.seed()` reproduces a run whatever `cores`.

| argument | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `center` | | the centre of the starts, or a parframe whose rows are the starts |
| `fits` | `20` | number of fits; the rows of `center` if it is a parframe |
| `samplefun` | `"rnorm"` | the sampler of the offsets, called with `n` and its own arguments |
| `startFromCenter` | `FALSE` | the first fit starts at `center` |
| `retry`, `nTries` | `TRUE`, `10` | a fit that fails starts again from the next draw, up to `nTries` attempts |
| `cores` | `1` | parallel fits, or `c(fits = , conditions = )` for threads over the conditions inside each fit |
| `optmethod` | `"trust"` | the optimiser, for example `"trustL1"` |
| `output`, `cautiousMode` | `FALSE` | write every fit to `resultPath/name/trial-<k>-<date>/` |

`msParframe()` draws a parframe of starts from a seed of its own, which leaves the global random
number generator alone; passed as `center`, it gives several runs the same starts, as in the
comparisons below. `load.parlist()` reads the fits that `output = TRUE` wrote, also of a run that
is still going or was aborted. Every fit in the result has its start `parinit` and its wall time
`elapsed`; a fit that failed is a list with its `error`, and the attribute `"run"` records the
optimiser and the sampler with their arguments, the cores, the times and the versions.

[Chapter 11](guide-remote-computing.html) runs the fits as an array job on a cluster, one fit per
task. `results/fits.rds` holds the result:

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !fitted}
cat("> Results pending: `results/fits.rds` of the project is written by `fit.R`.\n")
```

```{r load, eval = fitted}
```

```{r, eval = fitted}
head(fits[, c("value", "converged", "iterations")])
c(fits = nrow(fits), converged = sum(fits$converged), best = min(fits$value),
  withinOne = sum(fits$value < min(fits$value) + 1))
```

The waterfall sorts the fits by their final value, every fit, on a pseudo-log scale of the
distance to the best, which keeps the plateaus near the best apart and the far ones in view. A
plateau is a local optimum, and the number of fits on it shows the size of its basin of
attraction:

```{r waterfall, eval = fitted}
```

The parameters of the fits on the best plateaus, one colour per plateau. A parameter that differs
between plateaus is one the local optima disagree on; [chapter 5](guide-profiles.html) shows which
parameters the data determine.

```{r parameters, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 14, eval = fitted}
```

The prediction of the best fit against the data is the last figure of
[chapter 1](guide-model.html).

## Hessian sources compared

### The model of the guide

`optimizers.R` fits the model of [chapter 1](guide-model.html) with five sources of the model
Hessian from the same 100 starts, drawn as in the multistart above. The chain is built with the
reverse sweep and forward over reverse, as in [chapter 3](guide-sensitivities.html): Gauss-Newton
from the forward sensitivities, BFGS and SR1 from the reverse gradient and seeded with the
identity, the exact Hessian by forward over reverse, and 20 iterations of Gauss-Newton handing
over to BFGS, which starts from the Gauss-Newton Hessian at the handover. The fits ran as tasks
of a SLURM cluster with `distributedComputing()` ([chapter 11](guide-remote-computing.html)).

```{r optimizers, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !optimized}
cat("> Results pending: `results/optimizers.rds` of the project is written by `optimizers.R`.\n")
```

```{r, eval = optimized}
opt <- readRDS("results/optimizers.rds")
opt$method <- factor(opt$method, unique(opt$method))
top <- min(opt$value, na.rm = TRUE)
do.call(rbind, lapply(split(opt, opt$method), function(d) data.frame(
  starts = nrow(d), failed = sum(is.na(d$value)), converged = sum(d$converged),
  hits = sum(d$value < top + 1, na.rm = TRUE), iterations = median(d$iterations, na.rm = TRUE),
  seconds = round(median(d$elapsed, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
  secondsPerHit = round(sum(d$elapsed, na.rm = TRUE) / max(1, sum(d$value < top + 1, na.rm = TRUE))))))
```

`iterations` and `seconds` are medians over the starts, `secondsPerHit` the time of all starts over
the number of hits, starts that end within 1 of the best value of all; the plateaus of the
multistart above lie closer together than that. `failed` counts the starts that ended without a
result:

```{r, eval = optimized, fig.height = 6}
opt$rank <- ave(opt$value, opt$method, FUN = function(v) rank(v, ties.method = "first", na.last = TRUE))
ggplot2::ggplot(opt, ggplot2::aes(rank, value - top, colour = converged)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~method, ncol = 5) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(transform = scales::pseudo_log_trans(sigma = 0.1, base = 10),
                              breaks = c(0, 1, 10, 100, 1000, 1e4)) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = dMod_colors[2])) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "rank", y = "-2 log L above the best", colour = "converged") +
  theme_dMod()
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = optimized}
sens <- readRDS("results/sensitivities.rds")$timing
```

The cost of an iteration decides here. A reverse gradient costs about
1/`r if (optimized) round(sens[["forward"]] / sens[["reverse"]]) else 6` of the forward
sensitivities ([chapter 3](guide-sensitivities.html)), so BFGS runs more iterations than
Gauss-Newton in less time and reaches the best plateau from more starts: of the five sources it
needs the least time per hit. SR1 from the identity needs the most iterations of the single
sources and reaches the best plateau rarely. The exact Hessian converges most often, but an
evaluation by forward over reverse costs about
`r if (optimized) round(sens[["forward-reverse"]] / sens[["forward"]]) else 5` times the forward
sensitivities, and it needs the most time per hit. Gauss-Newton handing over to BFGS runs into the
iteration limit in most fits: the BFGS phase starts from the Gauss-Newton Hessian after 20
iterations, still far from the optimum, a seed whose excess curvature BFGS corrects slowly
([Seed and memory](#seed-and-memory)). The two published problems below show the same trade-offs
with other weights.

### Published problems

The sources of the model Hessian differ in what an iteration costs and in where a run ends. Two
published problems show how: the STAT5 dimerisation model of Boehm et al.
[@boehm2014identification] with nine parameters, the project
[boehmJProteomeRes2014](boehmJProteomeRes2014.html), and the JAK2-STAT5 model of Bachmann et al.
[@bachmann2011division] with 113, the project [bachmannMSB2011](bachmannMSB2011.html). Every
source of a comparison runs from the same starts, drawn once with `msParframe()`, so the runs
differ only in the method. A start is a hit when it ends within 0.1 of the best value. The cost
of a hit, the evaluations of all starts over the number of hits, combines the cost of a start
with the rate at which starts succeed.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !compared}
cat("> Results pending: `results/hessianSources.rds` of the Boehm project.\n")
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = compared}
boehm <- readRDS(boehmFile)
library(ggplot2)
# One panel for several fit collections, each ranked on its own, drawn back to front so that the
# first one listed stays on top. A circle is a converged fit, a triangle any other.
waterfall <- function(frames, cutoff = Inf) {
  ranked <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rev(names(frames)), function(set) {
    fits <- subset(frames[[set]], value < cutoff)
    fits <- fits[order(fits$value), ]
    data.frame(index = seq_len(nrow(fits)), value = fits$value,
               converged = as.character(fits$converged), set = set)
  }))
  ranked$set <- factor(ranked$set, levels = names(frames))
  colours <- stats::setNames(dMod_palette(8, "okabe")[-5][seq_along(frames)], names(frames))
  ggplot(ranked, aes(index, value, colour = set)) +
    geom_line(aes(group = set), linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_point(aes(shape = converged), size = 1.3) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 17), breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"),
                       labels = c(`TRUE` = "yes", `FALSE` = "no")) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = colours) +
    labs(x = "start, sorted by value", y = "-2 log L", colour = NULL, shape = "converged") +
    theme_dMod() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")
}
# hits within `tol` of `ref`, and what they cost
hitTable <- function(runs, ref, tol = 0.1) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(runs), function(source) {
    f <- runs[[source]]
    hits <- sum(f$value <= ref + tol)
    stops <- if (!is.null(f$stopReason)) f$stopReason else f$stop
    data.frame(source, best = round(min(f$value), 3), hits, starts = nrow(f),
               gradient = sum(stops == "gradient"), medianEval = stats::median(f$neval),
               evalPerHit = if (hits > 0) round(sum(f$neval) / hits) else NA_real_)
  }))
}
```

### STAT5 dimerisation

The nine parameters are on the log10 scale, with a weak prior of standard deviation 4 on the six
dynamic ones and bounds of $\pm 5$, as in `analysis.R` of the project. Two runs from the prior
centre, every parameter at $-1$:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
parlower <- structure(rep(-5, length(outerpars)), names = outerpars)
parupper <- structure(rep(5, length(outerpars)), names = outerpars)
start <- pouter
single <- list(
  gn = trust(obj, start, iterlim = 5000, parlower = parlower, parupper = parupper),
  "gn -> bfgs" = trust(obj, start, iterlim = 5000, parlower = parlower, parupper = parupper,
                       phases = list(list(hessianMethod = "gn"), list(hessianMethod = "bfgs"))))
```

```{r, eval = compared}
with(boehm, data.frame(source = names(single),
                       value = vapply(single, `[[`, 0, "value"),
                       stop = vapply(single, `[[`, "", "stopReason"),
                       neval = vapply(single, `[[`, 0L, "neval"),
                       qnEval = vapply(single, `[[`, 0L, "qnEval"), row.names = NULL))
```

Gauss-Newton stops on `"fvalue"`; the BFGS phase after it moves the value a little further and
ends on stagnation. The seeds and the memory of BFGS from the same start, a Gauss-Newton seed, the
identity, and the identity with `qnMemory = 10`:

```{r, eval = compared}
data.frame(seed = c("gn", "identity", "identity"), memory = c(0L, 0L, 10L),
           value = vapply(boehm$seeds, `[[`, 0, "value"),
           stop = vapply(boehm$seeds, `[[`, "", "stopReason"),
           neval = vapply(boehm$seeds, `[[`, 0L, "neval"))
```

From this start, several decades from the optimum, the Gauss-Newton seed keeps BFGS in the basin
Gauss-Newton ends in, the identity reaches the best optimum, and a memory of ten pairs, which
forgets the curvature of the earlier steps, ends far above. The cautious test of `qnCautious`
changes neither the outcome nor the cost on this model.

A multistart of 100 starts per source, five sources: Gauss-Newton, the two two-phase runs, and BFGS
and SR1 seeded with the identity.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(20260905)
starts <- msParframe(pouter, n = 100, sd = 3)
sources <- list(
  gn = list(hessianMethod = "gn"),
  "gn -> bfgs" = list(phases = list(list(hessianMethod = "gn"), list(hessianMethod = "bfgs"))),
  "gn -> sr1" = list(phases = list(list(hessianMethod = "gn"), list(hessianMethod = "sr1"))),
  "bfgs, id" = list(hessianMethod = "bfgs", qnControl = list(hessianInit = "identity")),
  "sr1, id" = list(hessianMethod = "sr1", qnControl = list(hessianInit = "identity")))
runs <- lapply(sources, function(settings)
  as.parframe(do.call(mstrust, c(list(obj, center = starts, iterlim = 5000, parlower = parlower,
                                      parupper = parupper, cores = 4), settings))))
```

```{r, eval = compared}
runs <- boehm$multistart
hitTable(runs, min(vapply(runs, function(f) min(f$value), 0)))
```

`gradient` counts the starts that ended at a stationary point, `medianEval` the evaluations of a
typical start. Gauss-Newton ends every start on `"fvalue"` or `"preddiff"`; the quasi-Newton
phases, where these tests are not applied, end on the gradient or on stagnation.

```{r, eval = compared, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "The five Hessian sources over the same 100 starts, each ranked on its own. Values above 600 are left out."}
waterfall(runs, cutoff = 600)
```

The curves fall into two shapes. Gauss-Newton and both two-phase runs follow each other over the
whole range, since such a run is Gauss-Newton until a soft stop fires. They differ in the leading
plateau: under Gauss-Newton it is not flat, because the model stops improving before the minimum,
whereas the quasi-Newton phase brings those starts to a common value. The runs seeded with the
identity form the second shape, with a longer leading plateau: they reach the best optimum from
more starts, and more of the remaining starts end high. Under BFGS this worsens the typical value,
under SR1 it does not. SR1 from the identity reaches the best optimum from several times as many
starts as Gauss-Newton, at a tenth of the evaluations per hit.

### Without the prior

The prior keeps starts away from the bounds and shapes the comparison. On the likelihood alone,
with bounds of $\pm 8$ and 200 starts, the published optimum is $-2 \log L = 276.44$
[@hass2019benchmark], and a hit ends within 0.1 of it. The two BFGS sources are left out, and two
others join: SR1 from a Gauss-Newton seed, and the reversed handover from SR1 back to
Gauss-Newton.

```{r, eval = compared}
noprior <- split(boehm$noprior, boehm$noprior$source)
hitTable(noprior, 276.44)
```

```{r, eval = compared, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Five Hessian sources on the likelihood without a prior, over the same 200 starts, each ranked on its own. Values above 600 are left out."}
waterfall(noprior, cutoff = 600)
```

Every source reaches the published optimum, and the quasi-Newton runs lose most of their lead:
SR1 from the identity reaches it from 32 of 200 starts against 34 of 100 with the prior, at seven
times the evaluations per hit, while Gauss-Newton gains, 28 of 200 against 6 of 100. SR1 from a
Gauss-Newton seed reaches the optimum from the most starts, and the reversed handover at the
fewest evaluations per hit, with a fifth to a quarter fewer evaluations per start than either SR1
run alone.

The reversed handover also changes how runs end:

```{r, eval = compared}
with(boehm$noprior, table(source, stop))
```

SR1 alone stagnates on most starts; handing back to Gauss-Newton turns that into ends on
`"fvalue"`, because the model tests of a Gauss-Newton phase apply again, and cuts the runs that
exhaust the iteration limit. The forward handover matches Gauss-Newton in hits and in runs at the
iteration limit, and differs in how its runs end.

### JAK2-STAT5, 113 parameters

The JAK2-STAT5 model of Bachmann et al. has 113 estimated parameters, 25 states, 20 observables
and 36 conditions; the fits ran on a SLURM cluster through `distributedComputing()`
([chapter 11](guide-remote-computing.html)), one job per source, each an array of 50 tasks of four
fits.

A multistart over 113 parameters needs a weak prior, or starts run into the bounds instead of
converging. The published values span twelve decades, and one prior centre for all, at standard
deviation 4, adds 27 to the objective at the published optimum and moves the optimum. The centre of
every parameter whose published value lies more than a decade from the default is the order of
magnitude of that value, so that it lies within one decade everywhere and the prior adds 1.04 at the
optimum. The optimum stays at the published parameters, where the objective with the prior is
$-479.26$; a hit ends within 0.1 of it. Starts are drawn around that centre with standard deviation
4 and drawn again where they leave the box.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !comparedBachmann}
cat("> Results pending: `results/hessianSources.rds` of the Bachmann project.\n")
```

```{r, eval = comparedBachmann && compared}
bachmann <- readRDS(bachmannFile)
bachmannRuns <- split(bachmann, bachmann$source)
hitTable(bachmannRuns, -479.26)
with(bachmann, table(source, stop))
```

```{r, eval = comparedBachmann && compared, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Five Hessian sources on the JAK2-STAT5 model over the same 200 starts, each ranked on its own. Starts ending above -400 are left out."}
waterfall(bachmannRuns, cutoff = -400)
```

Every source reaches the same best value, and the counts at 0.1 and at 1 from the optimum are the
same: a start either finds the published minimum or ends far from it. No source finds an optimum
another misses. The sources differ in cost: Gauss-Newton reaches the optimum at half the
evaluations per hit of the cheapest SR1 run, the reverse of the ordering at nine parameters.

For SR1 the identity is the better seed here, 79 hits against 65. The Gauss-Newton seed brings the
curvature of a point the run is about to leave into the first steps of an approximation that is
rebuilt anyway, and SR1 has no damping to discard it. After the forward handover the model tests no
longer fire and almost every run ends on stagnation, at the values Gauss-Newton reaches alone;
after the reversed handover most runs end on `"fvalue"`. Neither changes which optimum is found:
matched start by start, Gauss-Newton and the forward handover differ by $3 \times 10^{-6}$. By the
time a soft stop fires the basin is chosen, and the handover only changes how the run ends inside
it.

### Findings

The ordering of the sources depends on the problem. On the JAK2-STAT5 model Gauss-Newton reaches
the optimum at half the cost of the cheapest SR1 run; on the STAT5 dimerisation model SR1 is
cheapest, by an order of magnitude with the prior and by a factor of two without. The term
Gauss-Newton omits explains the ordering: where the residuals at the optimum are small, $J^\top J$
is close to the true Hessian, and a source that infers curvature from steps costs extra evaluations
without improving the model. Where they are large, so is the omitted term, the Gauss-Newton model
stops improving early, and its tests fire far from the minimum.

Three findings hold across the settings. No source reaches an optimum another misses; they differ
in cost. A handover does not change the basin a run ends in, since the basin is chosen before a
soft stop fires: the forward handover changes only where inside a basin a run stops, the reversed
one restores a valid stopping test. A quasi-Newton phase needs of the order of $n_\theta$ accepted
steps before it covers every direction, so its cost per hit grows with the number of parameters.

## L1 penalties

`trustL1()` minimises the objective plus an L1 penalty on some of the parameters,

$$f(\theta) + \sum_{i \in \mu} \lambda_i \lvert \theta_i - \mu_i \rvert ,$$

with the reference values `mu`, named by the penalised parameters, and the strength `lambda`, one
number or one per parameter. The penalty has a kink at $\mu_i$, where a parameter sits exactly
until the data pull it away with a force above $\lambda_i$; scanned over $\lambda$, it selects
which parameters differ from their references. `trustL1()` runs the trust region of `trust()`
with the Gauss-Newton Hessian of the objective and two changes:

- A penalised parameter on its kink is taken out of the subproblem while
  $\lvert \partial f / \partial \theta_i \rvert \le \lambda_i$: the penalty dominates, and the
  parameter stays.
- A step that moves a penalised parameter across its kink is cut back onto $\mu_i$, exactly, so
  that the next iteration examines it again and a zero difference is an exact zero.

`one.sided = TRUE` makes the penalty a wall, $\lambda_i \max(0, \mu_i - \theta_i)$. `gate` names
parameters whose penalty is $\lambda_i (\theta_i - \mu_i)$ with $\theta_i \ge \mu_i$: the parameter
sits on $\mu_i$ and leaves it upward only. `fuse` takes blocks of parameters penalised by their
differences, $\lambda \sum_{p < q} w_{pq} \lvert \theta_p - \theta_q \rvert$, plus optionally the
difference to an anchor: parameters with equal values move as one and split when the data pull
them apart, which groups conditions with equal parameters. The bounds are those of `trust()`, both
`boundary` settings included; of `tolControl` it reads `ftol`, `mtol`, `gtol`, `xtol` and `rmin`,
and of `stepControl` `thetaMax`. `mstrust(optmethod = "trustL1")` runs it from many starts.
[Chapter 8](guide-group-effects.html) estimates the differences between groups by a prior of the
random effects instead of a scan; the modes of its Laplace random effects come from `trustL1()`.

## Multiple shooting

Every method above integrates the model from its initial state across the whole time axis, single
shooting. For an oscillating or spiking system this makes the objective rugged: a small change of
a parameter shifts every later period, and once a peak has moved by more than its own width the
residuals no longer tell in which direction it moved. The valleys around the optimum become narrow
and the starts that reach it rare.

Multiple shooting [@bock1983recent; @baake1992fitting] cuts the time axis at nodes
$\tau_1 < \dots < \tau_M$. Segment $j$ is integrated from node values $s_j$ of its own, the first
one from the initial state the parameter transformation gives, and continuity becomes a
constraint of the fit,

$$c_j = x(\tau_{j+1};\, \tau_j, s_j, \theta) - s_{j+1} = 0 .$$

The nodes start at the data wherever a state is observed, so every segment stays close to its data
whatever the parameters are, and the gaps close only as the fit converges. At convergence the
trajectory is continuous and the result is a stationary point of the single-shooting objective.

In dMod2 multiple shooting is a control of the objective, not a different optimiser:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
obj <- normL2(data, g * x * p, multipleShootingControl = TRUE)
fit <- trust(obj, start)            # or mstrust(obj, ...)
fit$multipleShooting$violation      # the scaled gaps at the end
controls(obj, "multipleShootingControl") <- NULL   # single shooting again
```

Called as a function, `obj` is still the single-shooting objective, so evaluating, plotting and
profiling it are unchanged. `trust()` reads the control and runs the method below; a sum with a
prior keeps it. The chain has to be `g*x*p` with one prediction function from `Xs()`, built
on `odemodel(..., includeTimeZero = FALSE)`, so that a segment is integrated from its own start.
Not available with multiple shooting: `hessianMethod = "exact"`, more than one phase,
`switches`, `qnControl$hessianReseed`, `qnControl$qnMemory`, `stepControl$nonmonotone`,
`boundary = "clip"`, `minimize = FALSE` and `traceFile`.

### Condensed step

Bock's generalised Gauss-Newton method linearises the constraints at the current iterate
$(\theta, s)$. With $G_j = \partial x_j / \partial s_j$ and $P_j = \partial x_j / \partial \theta$
the sensitivities of the end state of segment $j$,

$$\Delta s_{j+1} = \alpha\, c_j + G_j\, \Delta s_j + P_j\, \Delta \theta ,$$

and the recursion from the first segment gives $\Delta s = \alpha z + S\, \Delta\theta$ for all
nodes at once. Substituted into the linearised residuals of the segments, it leaves a Gauss-Newton
model in $\Delta\theta$ alone (condensing). The subproblem keeps the size of the single-shooting
one, and the subproblem solver and the bounds above take it unchanged. The nodes follow the step
through the linearisation rather than a new simulation, so the gaps close as the iteration
converges, not at every point it visits.

The trust region bounds parameters and nodes together,

$$\lVert D\, \Delta\theta \rVert^2 + \lVert V (\alpha z + S\, \Delta\theta) \rVert^2 \le r^2 ,$$

with $V$ one over the scale of each state: the range of the data for an observed state, of a
simulation otherwise, and a decade for a state in a log10 chart (`multipleShootingControl$scale`
sets it). A region on $\theta$ alone does not bound $S\, \Delta\theta$, the linearised
single-shooting response of a node, which across a spike is huge. $\alpha = 1$ closes the
linearised gaps completely, Bock's own step. Under an active region the node step is damped with
the parameter step: $\alpha$ is the share of the node part of the full Gauss-Newton step that the
radius admits, at most one. Where condensing would propagate a gap through a chain of expanding
segments beyond a bound, that link of the linearisation is dropped for the step. A summand other
than the shooting term, a prior or a single-shooting `normL2()` of other data, enters with its own
value, gradient and Gauss-Newton Hessian.

A step is accepted by the filter of Fletcher and Leyffer [@fletcher2002nonlinear] on the pair of
the data term $f$ and the scaled gap size $h = \lVert V c \rVert$ (`stepControl$acceptance =
"filter"`, the default), or by the $\ell_2$ exact penalty $f + \mu h$ (`"merit"`). A rejected step
whose gaps did not close as predicted gets one second-order correction (`stepControl$soc`, on by
default), the trial gaps condensed with the sensitivities already at hand. A run reports
`converged = TRUE` only when $h$ has fallen below `tolControl$ctol`, and no other test ends it
before: with open gaps the nodes absorb what the parameters do not explain, and the data term is
no measure of the fit.

`hessianMethod = "gn"` condenses the Gauss-Newton block of every segment. `"bfgs"` and `"sr1"`
keep one quasi-Newton block per segment for the segment's Lagrangian, which gradients alone keep
up to date, and so run on the gradients of `sweep = "reverse"`.

### Continuity annealing

From a start far from the optimum, even the condensed step can be forced through a regime the data
never show, such as a spike threshold that the resting potential of the start never reaches.
`stepControl$anneal`, on by default, therefore first prices the gaps instead of enforcing them: it
minimises $f + w \lVert V c \rVert^2$ over parameters and nodes on the sparse Gauss-Newton matrix
of the full problem, with $w$ rising tenfold per stage from one, until the gaps are small, and then
hands over to the exact method. This is the precision annealing of variational data assimilation
[@ye2015improved] with a fixed schedule. A stage ends once a step gains less than a thousandth of
the objective, and the annealing ends early where the penalty dominates and a whole stage no
longer closes the gaps, where no weight will. It needs forward sensitivities and is skipped
without them.

### Nodes

`multipleShootingControl$nodes = "auto"`, the default, starts from ten segments per condition, or
from one per half oscillation of the data where that is more, and cuts a segment in two where

- the spectral radius of its propagation matrix $G_j$ exceeds `growth` (default 10). It is the
  factor by which the linearised flow of the segment expands, the same in every chart and under
  every scaling of the states;
- the root mean square of its weighted residuals exceeds `misfit` (default 3) and twice the median
  of its condition, where the model misses a feature of the data locally;
- or its solve fails.

This happens before the first step and at every iterate, never below half the finest spacing of
the data, and either half of a cut keeps `minPoints` data points, by default one more than the
model has states, so that no node can fit its segment alone.

The growth of an oscillator stays near one: along a limit cycle the flow neither expands nor
contracts, and a damped precession contracts. What grows over a long segment is the sensitivity of
its phase to the frequency, linearly with the number of periods it spans, and from a start with the
wrong frequency the phase slips by a whole period and the segment fits the data a period off. One
segment per half oscillation, counted at the turning points of the data, bounds that slip without
a look at the model. A misfit on every segment, as wrong parameters produce it, cuts nothing: no
node removes it, and cutting there would refine the time axis down to the spacing of the data.

An angle state goes on `charts = c(phi = "angle")`, where a gap counts modulo $2\pi$; `"log10"`
puts the node values of a positive state on the log scale. A state observed directly starts at the
data. The other states start at a run of the model whose observed states are reset to the data at
every data time, replacement synchronisation [@pecora1990synchronization]: states driven by the
observed ones, a gating variable driven by the voltage, forget where they started and follow the
measured trajectory, instead of being handed from one noisy value per segment to the next.
`init = "spline"` does the same with a smoothing spline through the data, its roughness chosen by
generalised cross-validation [@horbelt2002parameter], `init = "simulation"` takes every node value
from a simulation at the start parameters, and a list as `fit$multipleShooting$nodes` returns it
gives the node values, with the node times in `nodes`.

`nodes = "transitions"` puts a node just before every fast change of the data, a spike or the jump
of a relaxation oscillator, found as a run of samples whose rate lies more than eight median
absolute deviations off its median, and fills the rest with the even nodes of `"auto"`. The layout
stays fixed. Each change then starts in its segment where the data have it, whatever the parameters
are; the slow stretch behind it depends on them smoothly, and a wrong timing shows as a gap before
the next node, a small difference of the state rather than a change in the wrong place. Node times
given as numbers, for all conditions or as a list by condition, fix the layout as given.

### Further methods

Bock's own globalisation damps the full Gauss-Newton step, all linearised gaps closed, by a factor
that a curvature estimate predicts and a corrector cuts back; a damped step is taken when the
simplified step at its end, the Jacobians of the current iterate with the residuals and gaps of
the trial, has shrunk. This natural level function follows the geometry of the problem rather than
the weights of a merit function [@peifer2007parameter]; `stepControl$acceptance = "natural"`
selects it, with the filter taking over where the damping finds no step. It needs the Gauss-Newton
Hessian, a fixed sigma and no error model. Four further settings are off by default, since each
helps on some problems and costs on others:

- `stepControl$twoPhase` fits the parameters first with the node values held at their start
  [@horbelt2002parameter], then lays the nodes out afresh at the parameters found and releases
  them. Every segment has to explain its data from a start the data give, so no node takes up
  misfit the parameters should remove. This helps where noise in the node values would otherwise
  move the parameters, as on a spiking trace, at several times the cost elsewhere.
- `stepControl$regularise` holds directions of the condensed problem fixed whose singular value
  lies below that fraction of the largest, directions the data do not identify
  [@peifer2007parameter].
- `multipleShootingControl$breaks` names nodes at which continuity is not enforced
  [@voss2004nonlinear]; it needs the Gauss-Newton Hessian.
- `stepControl$restore` gives the filter its restoration phase, at most five times: it first
  closes the linearised gaps at the current parameters, damped if need be, and where that does not
  halve them puts the nodes onto the trajectory of these parameters. On a noisy spike train, nodes
  put onto the trajectory of wrong parameters let the automatic layout cut far more segments, and
  fewer starts reach the optimum.

The result has, besides the fields of a fit, a list `multipleShooting` with the final `nodes`, the
`gaps` per condition, their scaled size `violation`, the counts `nRelaxed` (iterations with a node
step below the full one), `nSOC` (accepted second-order corrections), `nSplit` (segments cut),
`nRestore` and `nStages` (annealing stages), the `cuts`, the `acceptance` and `sweep` used, `mu`
or `filterSize`, and with `blather = TRUE` a `trace`.

### FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillator

The FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillator [@fitzhugh1961impulses],

$$\dot V = c\,(V - V^3/3 + R), \qquad \dot R = -(V - a + b R)/c ,$$

is fitted to its voltage alone, 81 points on $[0, 20]$ with noise of 0.1.

```{r, eval = shotFhn, results = "hide"}
fhnDir <- file.path(tempdir(), "fitzhughNagumo")
dir.create(fhnDir, showWarnings = FALSE)
fhn <- eqnvec(V = "c*(V - V^3/3 + R)", R = "-(V - a + b*R)/c")
fhnModel <- odemodel(fhn, modelname = "fhn_ode", includeTimeZero = FALSE, compile = FALSE,
                     outdir = fhnDir)
fx <- Xs(fhnModel, options = list(atol = 1e-10, rtol = 1e-10))
fg <- Y(c(y = "V"), f = fx, modelname = "fhn_obs", compile = FALSE, outdir = fhnDir)
fp <- P(eqnvec(V = "V", R = "R", a = "a", b = "b", c = "exp(lc)"), condition = "C",
        modelname = "fhn_p", compile = FALSE, outdir = fhnDir)
compile(fx, fg, fp, output = "fhn", cores = 2)
fhnPrd <- fg * fx * fp

fhnTruth <- c(V = -1, R = 1, a = 0.2, b = 0.2, lc = log(3))
tt <- seq(0, 20, by = 0.25)
set.seed(1)
yy <- fhnPrd(tt, fhnTruth, deriv = FALSE)[[1]][, "y"]
fhnData <- as.datalist(data.frame(name = "y", time = tt, value = yy + rnorm(length(tt), 0, 0.1),
                                  sigma = 0.1, condition = "C"))
fhnSS <- normL2(fhnData, fhnPrd)
fhnMS <- normL2(fhnData, fhnPrd, multipleShootingControl = TRUE)
```

Forty starts perturb the initial states by a standard deviation of 1.5 and $a$, $b$ and $\log c$
by 1; each method runs from all of them:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(7)
fhnStarts <- parframe(do.call(rbind, lapply(1:40, function(i)
  fhnTruth + c(rnorm(2, 0, 1.5), rnorm(3, 0, 1)))))
fhnFit <- function(obj, ...)
  as.parframe(mstrust(obj, center = fhnStarts, cores = 4, iterlim = 300, ...))
fhnRuns <- list("single shooting" = fhnFit(fhnSS),
                "multiple shooting, filter" = fhnFit(fhnMS),
                "multiple shooting, merit" = fhnFit(fhnMS, stepControl = list(acceptance = "merit")))
```

A start is a hit when the single-shooting objective at its final parameters lies within 0.1 of
the best one. It is evaluated anew rather than read off the fit, since a multiple-shooting run with
open gaps reports a data term that can lie below the optimum.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !shotFhn}
cat("> Results pending: `vignettes/articles/results/fitzhughNagumo.rds`.\n")
```

```{r, eval = shotFhn}
fhnRuns <- readRDS(file.path(stored, "fitzhughNagumo.rds"))
fhnValue <- function(f) apply(as.matrix(f[, names(fhnTruth)]), 1, function(th)
  fhnSS(th, deriv = FALSE)$value)
fhnBest <- min(unlist(lapply(fhnRuns, fhnValue)))
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fhnRuns), function(method) {
  f <- fhnRuns[[method]]
  hits <- sum(fhnValue(f) <= fhnBest + 0.1)
  data.frame(method, converged = sum(f$converged), hits, medianEval = stats::median(f$neval),
             evalPerHit = if (hits > 0) round(sum(f$neval) / hits) else NA_real_)
}))
```

Multiple shooting reaches the optimum from more than twice as many starts, at a quarter of the
evaluations per hit. Much of what either method spends goes into the starts it misses: most of
those of single shooting run into the iteration limit, and the three starts multiple shooting
misses take almost half of its evaluations. The evaluations of a multiple-shooting run include
those of the annealing stages. One of them integrates every segment once, which covers the time
axis once as a single-shooting evaluation does, with the sensitivities of each segment's node
values on top of those of the parameters. The filter and the merit function reach the optimum from
as many starts at nearly the same cost.

### Pacemaker neuron

The pacemaker neuron of the pre-Bötzinger complex [@butera1999models] is harder. Its voltage fires
bursts of spikes about 2 ms wide. One burst, thirteen spikes in 700 ms sampled at 10 kHz with noise
of 0.25 mV, as a patch-clamp recording gives it, is fitted in the chart the symmetry reduction
certifies, with the voltage as the only observable. A change of a parameter by a per cent moves the
late spikes by more than their width, so the single-shooting objective breaks into narrow valleys,
one for every way model spikes can pair with data spikes. `bench/multipleShooting/preBotC.R` runs
the fits, half an hour on twenty cores, and stores what this section shows.

Two things decide the outcome besides the method. The solver runs at `1e-10`: at `1e-8`, far from
the optimum where misplaced spikes make the residuals large, the objective scatters by more than
the decrease a step predicts, and the trust region of either method collapses. And the nodes are
`nodes = "transitions"`, one just before every spike:

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !shotPreBotC}
cat("> Results pending: `vignettes/articles/results/preBotC.rds`.\n")
```

```{r, eval = shotPreBotC}
pb <- readRDS(file.path(stored, "preBotC.rds"))
round(pb$nodes, 1)
```

From the true parameters both methods reach the optimum, `ss` the single-shooting objective at the
end of each run:

```{r, eval = shotPreBotC}
with(pb$truth, data.frame(run, ss = round(ss, 1), gaps = signif(gaps, 2)))
```

From ten starts at each of three distances from the truth, the positive parameters perturbed on
log10 by `scale` and the potentials, half-activations and slopes by a fifth of that relatively, a
start is a hit when `ss` at its end lies within 1 of the optimum; `sec` is the median time of a
fit:

```{r, eval = shotPreBotC}
with(pb$starts, data.frame(method, scale, hits, fits, sec = medianSec))
```

`r if (shotPreBotC) sprintf("Single shooting reaches the optimum from %d of %d starts, multiple shooting from %d. The figure shows a start at %s decades: it stays silent, single shooting ends in one of the valleys with spikes too low and at the wrong times, and multiple shooting lays every spike onto the data.", sum(pb$starts$hits[pb$starts$method == "single shooting"]), sum(pb$starts$fits[pb$starts$method == "single shooting"]), sum(pb$starts$hits[pb$starts$method == "multiple shooting"]), pb$pick$scale)` A
miss of multiple shooting ends where single shooting ends, with spikes missing or added.

```{r, eval = shotPreBotC, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "One start, and the fits of single and multiple shooting from it, against the data (grey, every fifth point)."}
ggplot2::ggplot(pb$trajectories, ggplot2::aes(time, value)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = pb$data, size = 0.15, colour = "grey60") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = dMod_colors[1]) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~run, ncol = 1) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "time [ms]", y = "V [mV]") +
  theme_dMod()
```

Where the nodes sit decides. Ten even segments, the start of `"auto"`, contain several spikes
each: a small error of the parameters moves them, the segments miss their data, and the automatic
cuts pile nodes onto the spikes with the noise of the data in their values. A node just before a
spike leaves the spike in place and hands its timing to the gap in front of the next node, a smooth
function of the parameters. Close to the truth that turns a part of the starts single shooting
misses into hits; farther off the method is still a local one, and the hits fall with the
distance. The noise matters as well: with 1 mV at 1 kHz, one or two points on a spike, a node value
off by the noise just before the upstroke moves the spike by more than its width, and the
transition layout reached the optimum from none of fifteen such starts.

## Stored results

The comparisons of this chapter read stored fits; their code is shown above with the settings it
ran with.

- `examples/boehmJProteomeRes2014/results/hessianSources.rds`: the single runs, the seeds and the
  multistart with the prior, from the code above on the model of `analysis.R`, and the comparison
  without the prior, the fits of `bench/hessian/hessianSource.R` with the environment variable
  `BOEHM_NOPRIOR` set, minutes on one machine, reduced to source, value, evaluations, convergence
  and stop reason.
- `examples/bachmannMSB2011/results/hessianSources.rds`: the five sources on the JAK2-STAT5 model,
  five job arrays of 50 tasks of four fits each on a SLURM cluster.
- `vignettes/articles/results/fitzhughNagumo.rds`: the FitzHugh-Nagumo fits, from the code above.
- `vignettes/articles/results/preBotC.rds`: from `bench/multipleShooting/preBotC.R` with the
  environment variable `MS_RESULTS` set to the path of the file.
